extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of classical mechanics/fluid dynamics reproducing or applying Newton's theoretical and experimental results on fluid resistance
extracted.subtask_description: Deriving and measuring the resistance experienced by cylinders, spheres, and related bodies moving uniformly through a compressed, non-elastic fluid; includes theoretical scaling laws, geometric/channel corrections, assumptions, and experimental procedures for measuring resistance with falling spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma IV — Cylinder resistance independent of length (under uniform longitudinal progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cylindri, qui secundum longitudinem suam uniformiter progrediuntur, resistentia ex aucta vel diminuta ejus longitudine non mutatur; ideoque eadem est cum resistentia circuli eadem diametro descripti & eadem velocitate secundum lineam rectam plano ipsius perpendicularem progredientis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a cylinder whose motion is uniform along its length, increasing or decreasing its length does not change the resistance arising from its transverse section; therefore the resistance equals that of a flat circle of the same diameter moving with the same perpendicular straight-line velocity. (Used to reduce 3D problems to 2D cross-sectional considerations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XXXVII / Theorem XXIX — Cylinder resistance scales with velocity^2, diameter^2 and density ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Cylindrij ... resistentia, quce oritur a magnitudine sectionis transverscs, est ad vim qua totus ejus motus ... vel tolli possit vel generari, ut densitas medii ad densitatem cylindri quamproxime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resistance due to the transverse section behaves so that, for cylinders uniformly progressing in an infinite, compressed, non-elastic fluid, the resistance is proportional (approximately) to: duplicate ratio of velocity (i.e., velocity^2), duplicate ratio of diameter (i.e., diameter^2), and proportional to the ratio of medium density to cylinder density. Corollary 1 states resistance ratios compose from duplicate ratios of velocities and diameters and the ratio of densities. Assumes continuum, non-elastic fluid and neglects obliquity effects unless corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium — Obliquity of flow increases resistance; isolate cross-sectional resistance by removing oblique motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Obliquitas motuum ... retardat eorum transitum ... & resistentiam auget ... ut partes fluidi, quarum motus sunt obliqui & inutiles & resistentiam creant, quiescant ... & cohaereant & cylindrojungantur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oblique and indirect fluid motions around the body create additional resistance beyond that due purely to transverse section. To measure or reason about the pure sectional resistance, one must minimize obliqueness (e.g., conceptually 'freeze' surrounding fluid or otherwise prevent converging/diverging flows). The scholium prescribes imagining the peripheral fluid quiescent (or frozen) so only direct-through flow remains, thereby isolating the contribution from cross-sectional area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma V–VII — Shape equivalence under aligned axes and frozen peripheral fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: Si cylindruS, sphcera & sphaeroidS, quorum latitudines sunt aequales, in medio canalis cylindrici ita locentur successive ut eorum axes cum axe canalis coincidant : hae corpora fluxum aquae per canalem cequaliter impedient ... corpora predicta cequaliter urgentur ab aqua per canalem fluente.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given equal transverse dimensions and perfect axial alignment within a cylindrical channel (and under the hypothesis that surrounding fluid is rendered quiescent/frozen), a cylinder, sphere, and spheroid impede the flow equally; they are equally urged by the flowing fluid. This provides a criterion for comparing different shapes when axes coincide and peripheral disturbances are eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XXXVIII / Theorem XXX — Sphere resistance scaling (analogue to cylinder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Globuy in fluido compresso infinito & non elastico uniformiter progredientis, resistentia est ad vim, qua totus ejus motus ... vel tolli possit vel generari, ut densitas fluidi ad densitatem globi quamproxime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a sphere moving uniformly in an infinite, compressed, non-elastic fluid, the resistance relates (approximately) to the force that would stop/generate its motion over a characteristic path (here given as eight-thirds of the diameter) in the same proportion as the fluid density to the sphere density. Corollaries assert the same assembled scaling as for cylinders: resistance ∝ velocity^2 · diameter^2 · (fluid_density / body_density), with the sphere-specific geometric factor (eight-thirds of diameter enters the characteristic comparison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XXXIX / Theorem XXXI — Effect of channel/orifice geometry on sphere resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Globi per fluidum in canali cylindrico clausum & compressum uniformiter progredientis, resistentia est ad vim ... in ratione quae componitur ex ratione orificii canalis ad excessum hujus orificii supra dimidium circuli maximi globi, & ratione duplicata orificii canalis ad excessum hujus orificii supra circulum maximum globi, & ratione densitatis fluidi ad densitatem globi quamproxime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a sphere moves through a confined cylindrical channel, the resistance depends critically on the channel/orifice relative to the maximum circle of the sphere: the ratios involve the orifice area and the excess of that orifice above the semicircle of the maximum sphere cross-section (expressed algebraically via EF^2 and EF^2 − PQ^2). Thus channel aperture geometry (and its relation to the sphere size) must be included when predicting resistance; narrower orifices augment resistance according to the explicit ratios given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition XL / Problem IX — Experimental method for measuring resistance using falling spheres and logarithmic formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: Globi ... invenire resistentiam per phenomenia. Sit A pondus globi in vacuo, B pondus ejus in medio resistente, D diameter globi, F spatium quod sit ad D ut densitas globi ad densitatem medii ... G tempus quo globus pondere B sine resistentia cadendo describit spatium F, & H velocitas ... Et erit H velocitas maxima ... resistentia ... sequalis erit ejus ponderi B ... resistentia tamen in alia velocitate erit ad pondus B in duplicata ratione velocitatis hujus ad velocitatem illam maximam H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a concrete experimental procedure: drop spheres in fluid, measure descent times P (in seconds), use logarithmic computations (including constants/logarithms shown) to compute velocities, effective heights, and derive resistance. Key points: the maximum attainable velocity occurs when resistance equals the sphere's effective weight in fluid; resistance at other speeds scales as the square of speed relative to that maximum. Includes a prepared table mapping times to velocities and distances. Corrections for vessel geometry and finite depth are provided. This entry encapsulates the method to deduce inertial resistance from falling-sphere experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions about the fluid — continuity, compressibility, non-elasticity, and consequences for pressure propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluidum autem comprimi debet ut sit continuum; continuum vero esse debet & non elasticum ut pressio omnis, quae ab ejus compressione oritur, propagetur in instanti, & in omnes moti corporis partes aequaliter agendo resistentiam non mutet. Pressio quae oritur a compressione fluidi ... nullum generat motum in partibus fluidi continui ... ideoque resistentiam nec auget nec minuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All theoretical results assume a continuous fluid which may be compressible but not elastic, so pressure disturbances propagate instantaneously and do not create additional motions that would alter resistance. If the fluid were elastic or propagation not instantaneous, extra effects would arise and resistances would change. Thus applicability is limited to media approximating a non-elastic continuum (e.g., liquids approximated as non-elastic for these arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-channel / vessel-width correction (subduplicate ratio) for theoretical predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Si vasis latitudo non augeatur in infinitum ... effectus minuendi spatium in ratione quae componitur ex subduplicata ratione orificii vasis ad excessum orificii hujus supra semicirculum maximum globi & simplici ratione orificii ejusdem ad excessum ejus supra circulum maximum globi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experiments are carried out in finite-width vessels (not the ideal infinite channel), theoretical predictions must be corrected by factors involving subduplicate (square-root) ratios of the vessel orifice to the excess of that orifice above the semicircle of the maximal sphere. Practical computations (as in the experiments) apply these corrections to account for wall effects and limited channel aperture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental controls and common sources of error (guidance for reliable measurements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholium and experiment descriptions note procedures: freeze peripheral fluid to eliminate oblique motions; ensure spheres are thoroughly wetted/immersed to avoid buoyant acceleration from trailing parts; avoid adhered bubbles; account for wax rarefaction by temperature; avoid impulses from the releasing hand; minimize friction with the vessel walls; use sufficiently heavy spheres to reduce relative measurement error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for experiments: keep spheres cold (to avoid wax rarefaction and changing buoyancy), immerse completely before release to prevent initial impulsive effects from attached fluid, release gently to avoid imparting extra momentum, avoid wall collisions (choose large vessel width), and watch for adhering bubbles or other contamination. These controls reduce artifacts and make observed times agree with theory. The text reports experiments comparing computed and observed distances/times and discusses small discrepancies and their probable causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum velocity and its relation to densities and descent height
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocitas maxima quacum globus, vi ponderis sui comparativi, in fluido resistente potest descendere, ea est quam acquirere potest globus idem, eodem pondere, sine resistentia cadendo & casu suo describendo spatium quod sit ad quatuor tertias partes diametri suse ut densitas globi ad densitatem fluidi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The maximum steady velocity a body can attain under a given effective weight in a resisting medium is determined by a balance between weight and resistance and can be predicted by equating the space a freely falling body would describe (under no resistance) to a characteristic geometric length proportional to the densities (the statements give the proportionality). In practice one computes the characteristic height/velocity from the density ratio and compares experimental descent distances to assess resistance.
